notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on 2 Chronicles 20 from the sources I was able to access:

---

## 2 Chronicles 20 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — The Invasion Begins

After Jehoshaphat's return from Ramoth-Gilead and his reforms of civil and religious affairs, the Moabites, Ammonites, and Meunites (a tribe associated with Edom/Mount Seir, probably from the Maon region east of Seir) came to make war against him. The Hebrew text has a textual problem: it literally reads "some of the Ammonites" repeated, but by transposing one Hebrew letter, the likely original is "the Maonites" (Me‘ûnîm). Josephus calls them "a multitude of Arabs." — Ellicott; Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html); [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

Some see this invasion as an opportunity to exercise faith, not divine punishment, since it followed Jehoshaphat's reforms (2 Chron 19). Others note Jehoshaphat may have feared because the Lord had said wrath was upon him from the Ramoth-Gilead episode (2 Chron 19:2). — Precept Austin; Gill. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-20-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-20-commentary); [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

### v. 2 — The Report to Jehoshaphat

Messengers reported that "a great multitude" was coming from beyond the Sea (the Dead Sea). The Hebrew says "from Aram" (Syria), but Ellicott judges "Edom" to be the probable original, as Aram and Edom are often confused in Hebrew. The enemies had reached Hazazon-tamar (En-gedi), about midway on the western shore of the Dead Sea, roughly 36 miles from Jerusalem. — Ellicott. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

David Guzik notes the threat came after Jehoshaphat had returned to seeking God, following his near-death experience allied with Ahab. This "great multitude" was a significant threat to a king whose last battlefield experience was a narrow escape. — Enduring Word. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

### v. 3 — Jehoshaphat Fears and Seeks the Lord

Jehoshaphat was afraid — Gill says "exceedingly, as the Targum adds" — not merely from the enemy's numbers (he had substantial forces, 2 Chron 17:14), but because he remembered the prophet's word that wrath was upon him (2 Chron 19:2). Yet David Guzik argues "Jehoshaphat feared" means he feared the LORD, being more awed at God's power than at the enemy's. Matthew Poole is quoted: "Jehoshaphat feared; partly from human frailty, and partly from the remembrance of his own guilt." — Gill; Enduring Word. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html); [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

He "set his face to seek the LORD" — the phrase implies resolved determination (lit. "put his face"), used also in Daniel 9:3. He proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah, an act of national self-humiliation admitting guilt and seeking divine pity. — Ellicott; Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

Spurgeon preached that the case was "so altogether hopeless as far as they were concerned, that it was no use looking to anything beneath the skies … their immediate resort was to their God." — Spurgeon, via Precept Austin. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_2chronicles](https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_2chronicles)

### v. 4 — The Nation Gathers to Seek the Lord

Judah gathered "out of all the cities" to Jerusalem to seek the LORD at the temple. The word "seek" is a key theme in Jehoshaphat's reign, meaning both worship and discovering God's will; it shows trust in God over military resources. — Enduring Word. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

Spurgeon called this "What a prayer-meeting — a real one, a united one, with a definite object, and the king presiding!" — Spurgeon, via Precept Austin. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_2chronicles_pt2](https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_2chronicles_pt2)

### v. 5 — Jehoshaphat Stands in the Assembly

Jehoshaphat stood in the congregation in the house of the LORD, before "the new court." This name occurs only here and probably designates the great or outer court, recently repaired or enlarged (Asa had renewed the altar, 2 Chron 15:8). Gill suggests he stood on Solomon's brazen scaffold (2 Chron 6:13). — Ellicott; Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html); [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

### v. 6 — God's Universal Sovereignty

Jehoshaphat begins his prayer by affirming that Yahweh is God in heaven who rules over all kingdoms of the nations — no mere local or tribal deity. He has power and might so that none can withstand Him. Ellicott notes the parallel to David's prayer in 1 Chron 29:12 and Psalm 115:2-3. — Ellicott. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

Spurgeon: "When in time of trouble you ask help of God, ask it believing that he is able to give it; ask it expecting that he will bestow it." — Spurgeon, via Precept Austin. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_2chronicles](https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_2chronicles)

### v. 7 — God's Past Deeds and Abraham His Friend

Jehoshaphat recalls that God drove out the Canaanites and gave the land to the descendants of "Abraham Your friend." "Friend" (or "lover") is a title noted also in Isaiah 41:8 and James 2:23. Hebron, Abraham's burial place, is still known as el-Khalil, "the Friend." — Ellicott. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

Gill emphasizes the covenant aspect: since God gave the land as a deed of gift to Abraham's seed forever, will He now suffer it to be taken away? — Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

### vv. 8-9 — Appeal to Solomon's Prayer of Dedication

Jehoshaphat appeals to the temple and Solomon's dedication prayer (2 Chron 6:24-30). The summary: "If disaster comes … sword, judgment, pestilence, or famine — we will stand before this temple and cry to You, and You will hear and save." The unusual word "judgment" (shĕphôt) may be an ancient gloss for "wild beasts" as one of the four sore judgments, or the Vulgate understands "sword of judgment." — Ellicott; Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html); [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

Spurgeon said: "I like to plunge my hand into the promises, and then I find myself able to grasp with a grip of determination the mighty faithfulness of God. An omnipotent plea with God is: 'Do as thou hast said.'" — Enduring Word, quoting Spurgeon. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

### vv. 10-11 — The Injustice of the Attack

Jehoshaphat argues from God's own word: when Israel came from Egypt, God forbade them to invade Ammon, Moab, and Edom (Deut 2:4-5, 9, 19). Since Israel obeyed and spared them, it would be unjust for God to allow those same peoples to now drive Israel out of their inheritance. — Enduring Word; Gill; Ellicott. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/); [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

### v. 12 — "Our Eyes Are Upon You"

The climax of the prayer. Jehoshaphat openly confesses powerlessness: "We have no power … nor do we know what to do, but our eyes are upon You." Ellicott paraphrases: "We neither know nor deliberate upon a suitable plan of resistance, for our whole thought is centred upon Thee." — Ellicott. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

Martin Selman calls this "one of the most touching expressions of trust in God to be found anywhere in the Bible." — Precept Austin. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-20-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-20-commentary)

Spurgeon expanded: "They meant, 'Lord, if help does come, it must come from thee. We are looking to thee for it … We feel sure it will come, but we do not know how, so we are looking … as the servant looks to her mistress, so are we looking to thee.'" — Enduring Word, quoting Spurgeon. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

### v. 13 — The Whole Nation Before the Lord

All Judah stood before the LORD — including wives, children, and little ones. Gill notes they brought them so that the sight of their vulnerable families would stir them to fervent supplication, and also so that God would have compassion on the innocent. — Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

### v. 14 — The Spirit Comes Upon Jahaziel

The Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel, a Levite of the sons of Asaph, in the midst of the assembly. His genealogy is traced back five generations. Ellicott notes this is the only chapter where his name appears, and connects him with the Asaphite musical guild — Psalm 83, a prayer against a confederacy of Edom, Ammon, and Moab, is headed "A Psalm of Asaph" and may have been composed by this very prophet. — Ellicott. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

Gill notes the Spirit came "suddenly, while he was in the midst of the congregation … and perhaps had never prophesied before." — Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

### v. 15 — "The Battle Is Not Yours, but God's"

Jahaziel addresses all Judah, Jerusalem, and the king in a rising gradation. The core message: "Do not be afraid or dismayed … for the battle is not yours, but God's." Ellicott notes the echo of David's words to Goliath: "The battle is Jehovah's" (1 Sam 17:47). This was a real threat — there truly was a great multitude — yet the command was not to fear because God Himself would fight. — Ellicott; Enduring Word. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html); [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

**John Piper (Reformed Baptist)** emphasizes: "Jehoshaphat had cried to the Lord: 'O God, we are powerless! Help us.' And God responded, 'Fear not, the battle is mine!'" — Desiring God. [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ambushing-satan-with-song](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ambushing-satan-with-song)

### vv. 16-17 — Specific Directions and "Stand Still"

God gives precise intelligence: the enemy will come up by the Ascent of Ziz, and Judah will find them at the end of the valley before the Wilderness of Jeruel. Ellicott identifies the "ascent of Hazziz" as a pass leading up from Engedi to the desert table-land now called el Husâsah. — Ellicott. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

"You will not need to fight in this battle. Position yourselves, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD." This deliberately echoes Moses' words at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:13). Yet God still commands them to "go out against them" — a faith-partnership, not passive waiting. — Enduring Word. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

Ellicott notes the phrase "stand still" may be a marginal gloss explaining "set yourselves" (station yourselves, take your stand). The Targum reads "the Word of the Lord shall be your help." — Ellicott; Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html); [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

### vv. 18-19 — Worship and Loud Praise

Jehoshaphat bowed facedown and all the people fell before the LORD in worship. Spurgeon observed: "They worshipped, but why did they do it? They were not delivered. No, but they were sure they were going to be delivered." — Enduring Word. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

Then the Levites of the Kohathites and Korahites stood up to praise with a "very loud voice." Ellicott notes the Korahites were the leading division of Kohath — a guild of Levitical minstrels of the first rank, associated with the headings of many psalms (e.g., Psalms 44-49). The fact that Korahite Levites sang here corresponds with Psalms 46-48, which many scholars believe commemorate this very deliverance. — Ellicott. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

**John Piper** notes these were not merely "charismatic free spirits" but "the Choir of Israel," appointed since David's time to the ministry of song. — Desiring God. [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ambushing-satan-with-song](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ambushing-satan-with-song)

### v. 20 — "Believe in the LORD … Believe His Prophets"

Early the next morning they set out for the Wilderness of Tekoa (about 10 miles south of Jerusalem). Jehoshaphat exhorts: "Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld; believe His prophets, and you will succeed." Ellicott notes this is the affirmative form of Isaiah's words to Ahaz: "If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established" (Isa 7:9). To believe the prophets is equated with believing God Himself. — Ellicott; Enduring Word. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html); [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

### v. 21 — Singers Appointed Before the Army

Jehoshaphat consulted with the people and appointed singers to go before the army praising "the splendor of His holiness" (or, as Ellicott renders, "men praising in holy apparel" — Levitical vestments). They sang: "Give thanks to the LORD, for His loving devotion endures forever."

The singers leading the army was a dangerous step of faith: if God did not intervene, they would be slaughtered first. That is why Jehoshaphat consulted the people about who should volunteer. — Enduring Word. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

**John Piper's sermon "Ambushing Satan with Song"** is built on this verse: "What better way for Israel to meet the enemy than with songs of victory in the front ranks … When God tells us that the battle is his and that the victory is sure, the way we should meet the enemy is with songs of thanks." — Desiring God. [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ambushing-satan-with-song](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ambushing-satan-with-song)

### v. 22 — The LORD Sets Ambushes

"The moment they began their shouts and praises, the LORD set ambushes against the enemy." The Hebrew word for "ambushes" (ambushers) is slightly unusual, and some think these were supernatural agents (angels). Ellicott offers a natural explanation: a lurking band of Bedawi freebooters suddenly attacked part of the unwieldy host; in the ensuing confusion, the Ammonites and Moabites suspected their less civilised allies (the Maonites) of treachery and fell on them. The result was still providential — "the marvellous result, marvellously predicted, was brought to pass by a perfectly natural sequence of events." — Ellicott. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

Guzik notes: "It was not their praise that won the battle, rather it was their faith, yet their praise was sure evidence of their faith." — Enduring Word. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

**Piper**: "When they began to sing and praise, the Lord set an ambush against the enemy … The enemies of God are thrown into confusion by the songs of God's people. God has appointed the use of spiritual songs as an effective weapon against his archenemy Satan." — Desiring God. [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ambushing-satan-with-song](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ambushing-satan-with-song)

### v. 23 — Enemies Destroy Each Other

Ammon and Moab rose against the inhabitants of Mount Seir (the Maonites), devoting them to destruction, then turned on each other. Gill compares this to the Midianites in Gideon's time. — Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

The NIV Study Bible (quoted in Precept Austin) notes a key-word link: v.9 "we will stand before this temple"; v.17 "stand firm and see the deliverance"; v.23 "the men … rose up (lit. 'stood up') against the men from Mount Seir." — Precept Austin. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-20-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-20-commentary)

### v. 24 — Only Corpses Remain

When Judah reached a lookout over the wilderness, they saw only corpses; no one had escaped. The army of Judah never actually had to engage the enemy. — Enduring Word. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

### v. 25 — Three Days Gathering Spoil

They found an abundance of goods, valuables, and precious jewels — "more than they could carry away." Gathering took three days. Ellicott notes the LXX reads "cattle" (bĕhçmâh) instead of "among them" (bâhèm), suggesting livestock was among the spoil. The sheer quantity is explained because the invaders intended permanent settlement and brought all their goods with them (v. 11). — Ellicott. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

### v. 26 — The Valley of Beracah

On the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Beracah ("blessing") to bless the LORD. The place is still called Wady Beraikut, a wide valley west of Tekoa near the road from Hebron to Jerusalem. Jerome mentions a Caphar Barucha ("village of blessing") there. — Ellicott. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)

### vv. 27-28 — Joyful Return to Jerusalem

All Judah returned joyfully to Jerusalem with Jehoshaphat at their head, entering the house of the LORD with harps, lyres, and trumpets. The Targum reads "the Word of the Lord made them rejoice." — Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

### vv. 29-30 — Fear on the Nations and Rest for Judah

The fear of God fell on all surrounding kingdoms when they heard "the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel." Jehoshaphat's kingdom had peace, for God gave him rest on every side. Guzik notes this victory was a warning to neighboring nations and did not become a standing pattern for warfare; each battle required fresh leading from the Holy Spirit. — Enduring Word. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

### vv. 31-33 — Summary of Jehoshaphat's Reign

Jehoshaphat reigned 25 years from age 35. He walked in the way of his father Asa doing what was right. But "the high places were not removed; the people had not yet set their hearts on the God of their fathers." Gill explains these were not the idolatrous high places (those were removed, 2 Chron 17:6), but the ones where sacrifices were offered to the true God — the people could not yet be persuaded to worship only at Jerusalem. — Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

### v. 34 — The Source Document

The rest of Jehoshaphat's acts are written in "the Chronicles of Jehu son of Hanani" — the same Jehu who rebuked him in 2 Chron 19:2 — recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel. — Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

### vv. 35-37 — The Sinful Alliance with Ahaziah

Jehoshaphat allied with Ahaziah king of Israel, who "acted wickedly" (walking in the ways of Ahab, Jezebel, and Jeroboam). This occurred after the earlier rebuke for helping the ungodly (2 Chron 19:1-3), making it especially foolish. They built ships at Ezion-geber to go to Tarshish. The prophet Eliezer declared: "Because you have allied yourself with Ahaziah, the LORD has destroyed your works." The ships were wrecked.

Guzik suggests this was an act of divine mercy — God destroyed the ships to prevent Jehoshaphat from compounding his error. — Enduring Word. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

Gill notes that 1 Kings 22:49 says Jehoshaphat refused Ahaziah's servants after the ships were broken — this refusal came after the prophetic rebuke. — Gill. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)

---

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**On the nature of the "ambushes" (v. 22):**

- **Ellicott (Anglican)** argues for a natural-providencial explanation: Bedawi raiders sparked confusion leading to self-destruction — "a perfectly natural sequence of events," the prophet foreseeing only the issue, not the means. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)
- **Gill (Baptist)** and **Trapp** lean toward supernatural agents: "angels who appeared in the form of Edomites." Guzik notes "some have thought they must be supernatural agents." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html); [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)
- **Piper (Reformed Baptist)** applies the passage in a spiritual-warfare framework: singing as a weapon against Satan — "Ambushing Satan with Song." [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ambushing-satan-with-song](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ambushing-satan-with-song)

**On the "high places" (v. 33):**

- **Gill (Baptist)** distinguishes between idolatrous high places (removed, per 2 Chron 17:6) and those used for worship of the true God (not yet removed). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-20.html)
- The broader **Reformed** tradition (via Ligonier, not directly accessed) would generally see this as incomplete reformation — a failure to apply the regulative principle of worship requiring centralised worship at the temple alone.

**On "praise the beauty of holiness" (v. 21, BSB):**

- **Ellicott** renders this "men praising, in holy apparel" — meaning Levitical vestments — a translation difference with liturgical implications. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-20.html)
- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic)** reads it as praising God's holy beauty: "God's holiness — His 'set-apart-ness' — has a wonderful and distinct beauty about it." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/)

---

## Limitations

I was unable to access several desired sources due to tool limits: Pulpit Commentary full text, Dr. Constable's Expository Notes, Ligonier/Reformed sources, Catholic/Orthodox sources (newadvent.org, oca.org), modern scholarship sites (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org), Lutheran sources (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan sources (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), and the NT Gateway/GotQuestions treatments. Notes from these traditions could not be included.
